I’m a statistician who wants to build a career as a researcher in applied probability. I completed my Master’s in Statistics at McMaster University in 2026 under the supervision of Dr. Pratheepa Jeganathan, and I’m now applying to PhD programs in statistics.

Research interests: applied probability, particularly the ideas behind computational statistics and Bayesian nonparametrics. I hope to learn new concepts, develop my own, and encounter many more during a PhD.






My first experience of mathematical research started with a question I asked Dr. Noah Forman: does continuity of measure extend to uncountable unions of measurable sets? He conjectured that it holds for increasing families with an upper bound, then found a counterexample. I developed the proofs, learned the new mathematics the problem demanded, and formulated my own conjecture while exploring possible generalizations. The resulting paper, Counterexample to Continuity of Measure in Uncountable Unions, has been accepted in Examples and Counterexamples.
More importantly, this project showed me how much I enjoy theoretical work: developing rigorous arguments, understanding the ideas underneath them, and finding the next question to ask.



My Master’s thesis studied how sparsity from shrinkage priors interacts with structural identification constraints in Bayesian factor models. The goal was to recover the number of latent factors and the loading structure in high-dimensional settings with many irrelevant variables, motivated by the problem of uncovering latent structure in transformed microbiome data.
The main computational challenge was sampling the factor loadings and latent factors, whose conditional posteriors are strongly dependent. I developed a parameter expansion step for the MCMC sampler that introduces scaling parameters for the loadings and factors. With inverse-gamma priors on these scales, I showed that their conditional posteriors are generalized inverse Gaussian, so they can be sampled efficiently. I later rewrote the sampler in C++ and extended our simulations to settings with more variables than observations, where the UGLT structure gave the best predictive performance.
I presented this work at the 2026 Statistical Society of Canada Annual Meeting, and we plan to submit it to Computational Statistics and Data Analysis. This project taught me how to think about applied problems and gave me practical skills in simulation design and computational efficiency.




Two graduate courses shaped my interests most. Dr. Shui Feng’s Bayesian Nonparametrics course was built around the Dirichlet process. We would study a property of the Dirichlet distribution and see how it leads to a construction of the process: gamma random variables give the gamma construction, the Pólya urn gives a construction through de Finetti’s theorem, and the beta decomposition gives the stick-breaking representation, which connects to the Chinese restaurant process through the GEM distribution. Seeing one object built in several ways, with each construction revealing a different side of it, is exactly the kind of mathematics I want to spend my time on.
In Dr. Forman’s stochastic processes course, students delivered the lectures. I taught a set of lectures on martingales and their relationships to Markov, Wiener, and Poisson processes, including an introduction to stochastic kernels. Preparing them forced me to know the material well enough to answer any question my classmates asked, and I found I enjoyed helping them as much as deepening my own understanding. I’ve also worked as a teaching assistant for three statistics courses, from first-year help sessions to grading upper-year probability proofs.



I love learning with a reckless abandon. I like breaking complex concepts down and understanding them right from the ground up. If I had to build a house without knowing how, I would start by finding one (preferably abandoned) and taking it apart.



Made with ChatGPT 5


Why statistics? Truth be told, part of it, like all decisions, was chance (I’m going to refrain from making a probability joke here). I happened to stumble across a field with such depth that it keeps amazing me the further I go, and one where I can grow both by challenging myself mathematically and by improving as a programmer.



I want to do a PhD to learn new concepts, develop my own, and share that knowledge with others. Afterwards, I plan to pursue a faculty career where I can continue research in applied probability and teach alongside it.
In the meantime, I’m working full-time as a Risk Analyst at goeasy, where I test how machine learning risk models hold up when data goes missing.



The best way to reach me is by e-mail at 1simranbilkhu@gmail.com. You can also find me on GitHub and LinkedIn, or read my full CV.

title: Simranjeet Bilkhu
text:
Behold your luck! It seems that you have managed to find your way to my little site. My intention for this is to allow strangers to know me a little better, and for potential employers to assess whether my skills and interests align with what they are seeking.

I’m currently a Risk Analyst at goeasy. Before that, I completed my Master’s in Statistics at McMaster (June 2026) under the supervision of Dr. Pratheepa Jeganathan, where my thesis compared Bayesian factor models under PLT and UGLT identification constraints. I presented this work at the 2026 Statistical Society of Canada Annual Meeting, and I’m now preparing a paper extending it.

title: Simranjeet Bilkhu
text:
The Master’s was a great program. I (and hopefully my cohort) have acquired a lot of good practical skills in our modelling courses, both in coding as well as communication under the instruction of Dr. Ben Bolker. I’ve also been given great introductions to probability theory, stochastic processes, and Bayesian nonparametrics from none other than Dr. Noah Forman, and Dr. Shui Feng. I really have learned a lot taking this track, and perhaps I’ve learned an equal amount about myself. I began to realize why exactly I’m drawn to doing all this hard stuff; it’s because I love learning with a reckless abandon. I love breaking complex concepts down, and understanding things right from the ground up. Abusing this analogy, I would describe my learning process as follows:
Suppose I was given the process of building a house by myself. Of course, since I don’t have the current knowledge on how to build one, my task would be first would be to find a house (preferably abandoned), and start taking it apart.



Made with ChatGPT 5


So now the question is: why did I choose statistics as my main target of obsession? Truth be told, part of it, like all decisions, was chance (I’m going to refrain from making a probability joke here). I just so happened to be lucky enough to stumble across a field with such depth that it continues to amaze me the further I go. I love the fact that I can improve myself as a statistician by challenging myself mathematically, or by improving my programming knowledge.
These days I’m especially drawn to ideas in applied probability, such as those used in computational statistics and Bayesian nonparametrics, and I hope to keep exploring them during a PhD.
But of course, it’s good to have other passions asides from statistics as well. Along with projects and resources apt for my professional portfolio, you may find some sections of this site non-career related, so feel free to take a look!

title: Projects
text: Here are some projects that I’m pretty proud of. For now, I’m just adding projects that I completed during my Master’s degree at McMaster University.

title: Projects
text:
Papers


Master’s Thesis · 2026

A Comparative Study of Bayesian Factor Models under PLT and UGLT Identification Constraints
Supervised by Pratheepa Jeganathan.



Paper · Examples and Counterexamples

Counterexample to Continuity of Measure in Uncountable Unions
With Noah Forman. Also on arXiv.

title: Projects
text:
Talks and Presentations


Poster · SSC Annual Meeting · June 2026

A Comparative Study of Bayesian Factor Models under PLT and UGLT Identification Constraints
Presented my thesis research in the Student Research Poster Presentation Competition.



Talk · April 2025

Sparse Bayesian Factor Analysis when the Number of Factors is Unknown
A review of Frühwirth-Schnatter et al. (Bayesian Analysis, 2025), covering spike-and-slab priors, shrinkage priors and UGLT structures.



Talk

Reversible Jump MCMC
Background on reversible jump MCMC for models where the number of parameters is itself unknown.



Talk · January 2025

Sparse Principal Component Analysis
Links between factor analysis and PCA, and a simulation comparison of sparse PCA against varimax rotation.



Talk · September 2024

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
A conceptual and mathematical overview of HMC, plus a co-developed Shiny app for sampling with it.

title: Projects
text:
Modelling


Data Science · Winter 2025

Impacts of Diet Intervention on the Gut Microbiome
PCA and model-based clustering of microbiome counts with 1400+ features to compare plant- and animal-based diets.



Data Science · December 2024

Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Bird Migration
A spatio-temporal mixed model cut test error from 1,377 to 31 compared with ridge-penalised Poisson regression.



Data Science · November 2024

Establishing Baseline Climate Partitions via Clustering
K-means and agglomerative clustering of Canadian climate rasters, with the number of clusters chosen by silhouette analysis.



Data Science · September 2024

Expansion of Canadian Agriculture and the Relationship with Wetlands in Boreal Shield Provinces
66 satellite land-cover maps analysed in R, with a Shiny app to explore provincial trends.

title: Projects
text:
Probability Theory and Stochastic Processes


Lecture · July 2025

Martingales and Related Processes
Notes for a lecture I gave on martingales and their relationships to Markov, Wiener and Poisson processes, with an introduction to stochastic kernels.

title: Projects
text:
Bayesian Nonparametrics


Proof · Winter 2025

From the CRP to the GEM Distribution
A detailed proof that the proportions from the Chinese Restaurant Process converge in distribution to the GEM distribution.



Proof · Winter 2025

Size-Biased Permutations of the Poisson–Dirichlet Distribution
Showing that the size-biased permutation of the two-parameter Poisson–Dirichlet distribution is the two-parameter GEM distribution.
